Module 8

Enhancing Business Processes Using Enterprise Systems

A customer does not care which department is involved; they care that the promise is kept. This module follows one order across the departments that have to cooperate to fulfil it, then looks at the three systems built to make that cooperation ordinary: ERP inside the firm, SCM between firms, and CRM facing the customer. It ends by connecting the choice to Porter’s five forces and the value chain.

Learn by making the decisions

Each section teaches an idea and then asks you to use it. Nothing is graded and nothing is sent anywhere; every activity explains itself the moment you answer, including the options you did not choose. Work in this order:

  1. Follow the process. Lay out order-to-cash and procure-to-pay in the order they happen, and see what an out-of-order step costs.
  2. Place the work on the value chain. Decide which activity each system serves, and which gaps between them carry information badly.
  3. Choose the backbone. One suite or the best of each, which modules to configure and which to customize, and what the five-year bill actually contains.
  4. Look outside the firm. Run a four-tier supply chain, watch a small change in demand amplify upstream, and decide what sharing the signal is worth.
  5. Face the customer. Sort the work of a CRM into its components and decide what a single view of a customer is for.
  6. Make the strategy connection. Read the same evidence through the five forces and the value chain, then recommend one initiative and defend it.
  7. Test your understanding. The final challenge reports by objective so you know which section to reread.

Every organization, person, and figure used for practice is invented. Real companies appear only where the chapter itself uses them as examples.

Chapter vocabulary

Search the chapter terms or filter by objective. Each definition includes an example. Pay particular attention to the pairs that are easy to swap: order-to-cash against procure-to-pay, core against support activities, upstream against downstream, internally against externally focused systems, supply chain planning against execution, and a supplier portal against a customer portal.

Put it together

Final challenge

New situations ask you to choose and explain. Answer all questions, then score to see results by objective. Every business situation is hypothetical; use the missed questions to choose which section to reread.
foot:
Continue the practice. Take a company you know and follow one order through it end to end. Name the process, name the value-chain activity performing each step, and find the one handover where information has to be retyped, waited for, or guessed. Then say which of the three systems would close it, what it would cost to run rather than to buy, and what evidence would tell you a year later whether it worked.

Reading basis. Supplied Chapter 8, learning objectives 8.1–8.5: core business processes and organizational value chains; enterprise systems; enterprise resource planning; managing supply chains; customer relationship management. Framework applications draw on Porter’s strategy concepts. All practice organizations and figures are invented; vendor prices, market shares, and chapter forecasts are not presented as current facts.
